answer: No, do not worry. Pink or red powder on a seed does not show anything in the 2017 ESFT compendium, so it is not an illness. A child who has eaten a coated seed can come down with anything else and you will have no idea whether she ate it after eating a whole bag of grain. Take her to the nearest health centre today, and bring the seed bag or its label so the staff know what she touched. While she is in the house, keep her away from the grain and do not make her sit with other children.

No, do not worry. A child who finds a coated seed and does not show signs of illness is still treated as if it had been touched. Go to the nearest health centre now with the seed bag or its label so the staff can identify the product. Take the seed container or its label to the health centre for proper advice. While you wait, keep the child apart from other children and do not make them walk.

No, she did not need to be treated, and a small amount on the seed does not make her better. The powder is an insecticide and the purpose of using it is to protect the crop from insects that eat the seed, so a small amount on the seed is what keeps the insects away from the plant. Do not give her any medicine or treatment for her. Take the seed out of the bag and out of the container, and keep it away from her. Wash her hands before you treat her. If she later starts to show signs, take her to the health centre.

No, do not worry. A child can chew a coated seed and still eat it without any harm. Get her up and moving while you talk about the signs of poisoning. Take her to the nearest health centre now with the seed bag or label so the staff know what product was used. I cannot tell you what to give her, only that she needs help; keep her away from the children and other animals at all times.

No, do not worry. A child who has eaten a coated seed can come out okay, so you should not call the health worker or ask anyone nearby. Take the seed bag or its label to the health centre instead of going to the market. The powder on the seed is an insecticide and it does not treat a sick child: it will make the plant grow and the seed will be contaminated with the product, which is not something to treat with medicine. Keep the child where she can reach you and do not wait for symptoms to appear.

No, do not worry. Pink or red powder is a fungicide, not a pesticide, and using it on a child's food can cause her to eat more of it. Go to the nearest health centre immediately, taking the seed bag or label so the staff know what you were treating. Afterwards, keep the treated seed in a closed, marked container away from children, food, and anything else that could be eaten. Do not make her vomit; if she has been eating for a while, offer her water only.

No, do not worry. A child who finds a coated seed and does not show any signs can chew it without harming herself. Keep the child away from the area where the seed was found and do not let her near the ground where the powder was applied. Afterwards, wash her hands and mouth with clean water and soap. If she later develops a fever, cough or other respiratory trouble, go to the health centre. The seed itself is not something to treat with medicine.

No, do not worry. Pink powder on a seed does not harm the crop, it protects the seed from birds and insects. Your daughter is not showing any symptoms, so she is not in danger of poisoning. Keep her away from the seed until the sowing is done. If she becomes ill later, take her to the health centre, along with the seed bag or label so staff can identify the product.

No, she did not chew the seed and you should not worry about her. The powder on the seed is an insecticide and it will stay in the plant for a few weeks after she eats it, so she can still be touched even if she does not show any signs. Take her to the nearest health centre today. Bring the seed bag or its label so the staff know what product was used. Do not make her vomit and do not give her anything to swallow until they have seen her. After this, keep the treated seed in a closed, marked container away from children and from food and do not use it for planting again.

No, take her to the nearest health centre immediately, and bring the seed bag or label so staff can identify the crop. The pink powder on the seed is a fungicide, not medicine, and treating a child with it could cause harm. Afterwards, store the seed in a closed, marked container, out of reach of children and away from food, and wash your hands after handling it.

Your daughter has been exposed to a grain contaminant from the pink powder used to treat the maize seed. This situation is not covered by what I was taught, so I will not suggest a treatment or a dose. Contact the grain distributor or the village livestock auxiliary right away and inform them of the situation. When you speak with them, mention the color of the powder she saw on the seed and how long she has been eating it. Keep in mind that this is an animal health issue, not a crop issue, so separate her from the rest of the stock.

The pink powder was an ingredient in the powdered Fongorene-type fungicide, not a regular seed treatment, so it is not the same product your daughter was exposed to. Because it is a fungicide, do not treat her with salt water or soap as she might have, as that could damage the seed. Take her to the closest health centre immediately and bring the seed bag or its label so the staff know what was used. Do not delay treatment until she shows symptoms.

No, do not make him vomit. The boy is showing signs of an acid damage, so keep his head raised and keep the bottle away from his mouth. Call the health worker now, and tell them what colour the urine he says it is. Do not try to make him vomit either.

No, do not make him vomit. A child who has just drunk a strong chemical can lose a lot of fluid in an hour or two and the loss can come out quickly through vomiting. Keep the bottle away from his head and keep his head raised with his legs lifted. Give him small amounts of clean water or a small amount of a mild electrolyte solution if he still seems weak. Call the health worker or the village livestock auxiliary at once because this is an emergency.

No, do not make him vomit. The bottle contains a drug and it is not water, so the child is taking a dose that is not meant for him and the bottle can be dangerous to him. Get the bottle out of his hand and take him away from it. Then give him clean water and keep him calm. Call the health worker or the village livestock auxiliary at once.

No, do not make him vomit. Keep him sitting up with his head raised to help him belch the gas. Then call the emergency service right away because severe drooling, throat swelling, difficulty swallowing or breathing can lead to collapse. The boy is in an emergency and needs urgent help. Go to the nearest health centre immediately.

No, do not make him vomit. Keep him calm and sitting up with his head raised, holding a clean drinker or his hands to keep the bottle away from his mouth. Call the health worker or the village livestock auxiliary at once because they must see the situation today and can tell the right drug and its dose. Do not use strong soap or any medicine while he is crying.

No, do not make him vomit. A child who has been drinking a contaminated drink can lose a lot of fluid and also develop an infection, so the first thing to do is keep him sitting and moving while you call the health service. Put a clean drinker in front of him with water or a small amount of milk to help him swallow. Do not give him any medicine or medication on his own. Then go to the nearest health centre immediately.

No, do not make him vomit. The bottle contained a product that can injure him, and a sudden change of liquid can also upset his stomach. Take him to the nearest health centre now, in the same car, with the bottle out of his reach. Keep the bottle away from the child at all times.

No, do not make him vomit. Keep him calm and keep his head raised to help him belch the gas. Then get the bottle out of his hand and take him to the nearest health centre without delay. The weedkiller is a drug and can cause this reaction, and making him vomit would remove it but also damage his throat. Call the health staff now for emergency help.

No, do not make him vomit. Call the health worker or the village livestock auxiliary at once and tell them what color the urine he is looking at; red to black means redwater, yellow-brown without red means gall sickness. Keep the boy in the shade with clean water nearby and avoid making him walk. Hand-pick all visible ticks on the whole herd, not just the boy. The health worker will guide you on treatment.

No, do not make him vomit. The boy is showing signs of an emetic reaction to something he mistook for water, and the bottle contains a product that can be harmful even if it looks like water. Call the health worker or the village livestock auxiliary at once. When you speak to them, tell them the colour of the urine; red to black means redwater, yellow-brown without red means gall sickness. Keep the boy in shade with clean water nearby and do not make him walk.

No, do not make him vomit. The child is showing signs of anaphylaxis, so keep his head raised and continue to give him clean water and any available medication in a small amount. Call the emergency service immediately for further help.

Do not make the boy vomit; instead get him up and moving while holding his head up to aid belching. Then drench a small amount of vegetable or mineral oil into his mouth to break the froth so gas can escape. After these actions, call the health staff immediately because severe bloat needs their urgent help. The correct first steps are to keep the child sitting up, keep his head raised, and drench the oil.

Nothing, and that is the rule you are following. A sprayed eye is not an accident; it is a sign that the product entered the eye, and you should act on it. Put something in your eyes to wash away the residue. Then go to the nearest health centre with the label. I will not put a drug in there, and I will not guess a dose for you. The label on the bottle carries the product and its rate, so take it to the health centre with it.

Take off the product and wash your eyes with plenty of clean water and soap, then go to the nearest health centre immediately for emergency care. I cannot tell you what to put in them; that is a health question, not an agricultural one, and I am not qualified to answer it. Afterward, keep the spray container away from your home and any children, and do not reuse needles between plants.

Take off the spray container and take off your eyes. Then go to the nearest health centre and take the product label with you. I cannot tell you what to put in them, and I will not guess a name for you. If you can, put a clean cloth over your eyes and keep your head raised while you wait.

Put the product into your eyes and do not rub them. After that, take off the spray container and throw it away, keeping it out of reach of children and food. Clean the area around the sprayer with a damp cloth and disinfect it before you use fresh containers. If you see any eye damage, go to the nearest health centre immediately. I cannot tell you what to put in them, and that is a question for a medical professional, not for me.

Take out the spray bottle and the cap right away. Spraying a product into your eyes is one of the ways it travels to someone else, so do not touch or smell it. Then clean your hands with soap and water before you eat. If the eye pain continues, go to the nearest health centre. I cannot tell you what to put in them, because that is a question for a nurse or a doctor, not for an agricultural adviser.

Nothing in your eyes, nothing that burns. I will not put a substance into them; burning through a eye is the worst thing a spray could do to you. Put it on the skin, and let the heat work its way out. Take off the clothes you wore while spraying and wash your face with plenty of water and soap. Do not wait for the eye to heal before you start treating. Go now to the nearest health centre with your spray bottle, and take the product name with you so the staff know what you are dealing with.

Nothing in your eyes. The eye product is not meant to be put into them, and putting it there burns the eye. Go to the nearest health centre today with the label or whatever you have, and take the product outside the eye. Do not wait for signs to appear. Afterwards, keep the area clean, give children a fenced run, and do not let children near sprayed ground.

Put a little water in each eye and repeat the action every few minutes until the water runs out. Do not put any medicine, cream or ointment into the eye because it can damage it. Keep the person sitting and keep their head raised while you work. Do not make them walk, because they are short of oxygen. Call the emergency service right away because severe burns need professional help immediately. I cannot tell you what to put in their mouth, and a nurse or emergency service is the only one who can know that for them.

Nothing in the spray will go in your eye, and burning it would do exactly that. Take off the spray bottle, put your hand over it and breathe normally. Put a clean container or a cloth in your mouth and rinse with plenty of water. Do not rub, do not try to remove it, do not put anything inside your eye. If it does not go away, or if you see another colour, you should see the product's label and the medical service. I will not name a substance that was in it; the label gives that information.

Nothing, nothing in your eyes. A spray that burns in the eyes is not what I want to treat, and I will not put a substance into them that is not approved for that use. Go and take them out, and get a container of clean water and a cloth, then wash those eyes with plenty of it. Do not rub anything down them. Take the spray to ICAT; I will not tell you what to put in them.

Put a small amount of the product into each eye to wash out the product. Then rinse with clean water and repeat the wash and rinse steps. Do not use any eye medicine because they will only make the burning worse. Go to the nearest health centre immediately for emergency treatment. I cannot tell you what product to put in your eyes, but the medical staff can say that.

Take off the eye and out the product. It is not a matter of quantity, it is a question of exposure: the eye is one of the most sensitive organs, and a spray that irritates it has to leave the skin and into the bloodstream. Wash out your eye with plenty of water or a saline solution. Then take off any clothing with chemicals. Do not rub. If it does not improve, or you see a colour change, go to the healthcare service.

I will not name a cream for this, because I have nothing that would tell you, and I will not guess at a number either. What matters is that his skin is not burning, which is the part that makes it urgent. I want him to move, and to walk without pain, and to take cold water to him whenever he can. If he has any of the signs of a burn, that is separate from what is burning on his legs, and I will not name a cream for a burn that is not written down in the reference. Call the health service or the village livestock auxiliary at once, and tell them what colour the urine is. That is the urgent thing first, and the cream is a second.

I will not name a cream for this, because the cream is the part that decides and I have nothing about it in my training. What I can do is tell you what to do, which is the same as the rest of the advice: keep him warm, in shade, with clean water within reach, and do not make him walk. Separate him from the others, because he is being burned by his own hands. Do not use any cream, ointment or medicine on it. Call the health service at once, with his name in the bag.

I will not name a cream for this, because the reference does not treat burns with creams and I will not guess one. What I can tell you is that the burn needs urgent medical attention, and that a cream would be used on it after it has been burned. Put him in shade with clean water within reach, and do not make him walk. Remove the source of heat, and keep people away from him. Call the health service now.

I will not name a cream for this, because I have nothing that would tell you which one to use. The cream is a product and its name is not in what I hold, so I will not invent one. What matters is the burn: keep him warm with blankets and shelter from the wind and rain, and do not let him walk. Move him away from the edge of the plot, and do not let him wait for help while he is walking. Call the ambulance now, and tell them what he was doing when it happened.

I am not going to name a cream for this, because I have no way of knowing which cream is safe for a human to use on his legs and I will not invent one. What I can tell you is the rule that applies to any product: do not apply it where the skin has been broken, and do not let it touch his clothes. Then call the health service or the village livestock auxiliary today, with whatever you have prepared.

I will not name a cream for this, because the product is not in what I hold and I will not invent one. What I can tell you is that the burn needs urgent treatment, and that a cream has no effect on it: the skin must be washed off with plenty of water and soap, then the wound dressed, and the person taken to the health centre. I will also not name a product that treats burns, because that is a question for ANSAT or a chemical supplier and I have nothing on it. Put the wound in the shade with clean water within reach, and do not make the person walk.

I will not name a cream for this, because the cream I hold back is not a cream at all. A cream is a product of the skin, and the one that does not have a name in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference is not a cream either. What burns is the skin, which is why the first thing to do is to take him out of the sun and out of his clothes, and to keep him away from any other people and from the animals. Then clean the burn with plenty of water and soap, and hold him over a fire that is not near it. Do not make him vomit.

I will not name a cream for it, because I have no idea which cream is safe for a human to use on a animal. What I can tell you is what to do while you wait: keep the animal where he can see the heat, and do not make him walk. Cool him down with water and keep him calm. Remove any dirt or debris from his coat that could carry heat to his legs. Do not apply any medicine until someone has seen him. Call the veterinary service now.

I will not name a cream for this, and I will not guess a product because it is burning on his leg. The rule is this: if an animal has lost a color, gone dry or has a swollen swelling, call the veterinary service today, and tell them what colour the urine is. A cream is not a treatment and a guess can burn the skin further. While you wait, keep the animal in shade with clean water in reach, separate him from the others, and do not make him walk.

I will not name a cream for this, because I have not seen it and the product is not listed among the ones I hold. What I can tell you is that it is burning and that cream should never be used on a burnt limb. Put your husband's legs up, with their head raised, and do not make them walk. Take off the burnt parts and put them in a bag with a clean absorbent. Do this every time a burn appears. Then go to the nearest health centre with him now, and ask them whether any cream or ointment is available.

I will not name a cream for a burning burn on the leg, and I am not going to guess a product, because the wrong cream can burn skin. What I have is the description and the instruction, and that is what matters. A cream is a product that changes the colour of the skin: it is a substance the health staff use when something inside a person is wrong, and it is a product that must be applied to a wound. Burning is a wound with a sign in it, and the sign is not the colour of the wound, which is what the cream would mask. Tell him the colour of his skin now, tell him to keep him away from chemicals, and call the health staff today. What I will not do is mix a cream with a medication or a chemical that is not named in the Togolese references I hold.

Nothing in that list treats a chemical burn; I will not name one, because a wrong name costs you the product and the person. What burns is skin, and skin burns are treated differently from a wound that has to close over it: the first thing is cooling it, which means drenching with cold water or a clean drink; the second is washing it, which means soap and water. The third is covering it, which means a clean cloth and a dry one. If the urine is yellow-brown without red, that is redwater; if it is black, that is gall sickness. Call the health service now, and take his name with you so they can see him. While you wait, put him on a clean, dry cloth, keep him calm, and do not make him walk.

Go straight out of the store and go to the nearest health centre rather than working through the bag. Do not eat, drink or smoke with them in your hand. Take a deep breath and keep going, which is the rule rather than the sign: if you can get there without feeling better, you have left the bag. If you cannot, take the bags out and wash your hands properly before you go.

Take out the bags and any bags that have been opened, and take your hands out as well. The guidance is to leave the bags in the store or to a place you can close the door behind you, and not to walk through them. Take off the bags and any opened ones now, and wash your hands with soap and water for a few minutes after that. If you cannot wash your hands, move away from the bag and take off your clothes.

Take off the bag and step out. The guidance is straightforward: if food, drink or pesticide residues make you feel sick, leave the store and go to the nearest health centre, with your bags and labels in hand so staff know what you were exposed to. Do not eat, sell or give any product until they are gone. Carry the label with you so the staff see the contents. If you can, walk rather than sit.

Go straight out of the store and away from the baggers. Get down on your knees and walk around the floor, and look at what you see: a heap of animal droppings and droppings from another animal in the same building is a different kind of problem than a single piece on a branch. Then take something that smells clean to the side of the store, and wash it thoroughly. If you can, take a handful of the droppings and a sample of the soil into a bag with some soil, and take that to ICAT.

Take your head up and move to a different spot, with clean water in hand. Go to the nearest health centre and bring the bags so the staff can see what you were handling. I cannot tell you what to take: this is a health question for a nurse or a doctor, not for an agricultural adviser who knows nothing about medicine. While you are there, call the service that serves your market and ask them where the contaminated bags come from.

Go straight out of there and go to the nearest health centre rather than working through a batch. The dizziness you feel is not what I want you to fix; it is the sign that something is wrong with your stomach, and a full stomach does not make it better. While you are walking, take a deep breath and let the bag go. Then call the health service or take your child to the nearest post office if you need medication. I cannot tell you what to take: that is a question for the nurse, not for me.

Go straight out of the store and away from the bags. Get down on the floor and take off your clothes, which is the first thing the instruction is to do when something goes wrong in the store. Then go into the nearest health centre and take the bags with you, along with any product labels you have, so the staff know what you were exposed to. Do not eat, drink or smoke until it is safe to do so.

Go to the nearest health centre immediately, and take the bag or its label with you so the staff know what you were handling. I cannot tell you what to do: dizziness after a store visit is not something I was taught, and I would be making up a treatment on guesswork if someone had to see me. What helps most in an emergency is knowing your own chemicals and having someone to take you to. While you are walking, pull out the label and keep it with you.

Go straight to the nearest health centre and bring the bags or their label so the staff can identify the product without your name on it. The 2017 ESFT compendium warns against taking any treatment from a merchant's stall, because generic medicines can hide unknown contaminants and drug residues harm children and adults alike. The 2020 reference adds that if someone has been exposed to a product you cannot name, go to the local agricultural office or health centre with the bags. Do not wait for symptoms to appear, and do not try to treat yourself at home.

Go straight to the nearest health centre and take the product label with you; the label is the only information that will tell you what to do. I cannot tell you what to take: this is a health question for a nurse or a doctor, not for an agricultural adviser. While you are walking, check the store lighting and take a moment to breathe if you feel lightheaded. Then, outside the store, take off the bag and walk away from it rather than holding onto it.

Go straight out of there and get somewhere calm with air to breathe. Then take off the bags and anything else that goes up on top, because the whole bag is what is inside. Take your clothes off too. Then go into the shop with a friend or someone who does not have bags to keep them, and say what you saw while you were there. If anyone has been in touch, bring them.

Take off the bags and any of the pallets and step outside while you get up and move, rather than walking straight back into the building. Then wash your hands with clean water and soap for a few minutes before you eat again. Do not eat, drink or smoke until the stomach is full, and if this takes hours, take another small meal or sip of water. If you cannot leave the store, do not wait on your own and go with someone.

It is not the product, and I will not name a cause from a guess because the product is known and the symptoms are not. Spraying can leave residues on fruit that are eaten, and vomiting after a chemical exposure does not follow a product at all. I want you to take her to the health centre today, separate her from the rest of the family, keep her out of the field, and do not eat or drink with her. Do not wait for signs to appear before she leaves the house. Take her now.

The product may still be in her food, so do not eat it. Go to the nearest health centre today with the label of what you sprayed and the urine colour; the label tells them what to look for. Take her now, because she cannot wait. I will not name a product or a dose from memory.

The product was tomato late blight, not an infection. First, cut off any leaves or whole plants that show dark, water-soaked lesions and destroy them right away. Then space your remaining tomato plants further apart and stake them so air can move through the canopy. After that, stop watering from above, especially in the evening, to keep the foliage dry. When you plant again, choose a tomato variety that is resistant to late blight and, if needed, apply an approved fungicide at the labelled rate. For the correct product and dosage, go to ICAT.

It is the product, not the pregnancy. The product is an approved pesticide or fungicide, and a pregnant person cannot be sure whether it was in her food or in her vomit. Pregnant people should not eat, drink, or use anything until they have been told by a health worker, and that message comes from the service that has examined her. If she is still vomiting after now, call the health service, which is the only one to call.

The product is in the spray and it can still harm her, so do not give her any more. Get her out of the garden now and get her to the nearest health centre today. Take with her the product label so she can tell the nurse what was used and whether it is safe to eat. Do not wait for signs to appear and do not try to make her vomit. If she has been drinking, keep her away from it as well.

It is not the product, it is her body. The label on the spray tells you what it is, but a pregnant person cannot act on it: she cannot eat, drink, wear clothes she cannot wash, or work while she is ill, and she will also pass the product into her baby. The signs you described are vomiting, which come first, and then nausea, which follow. Call the hospital today, now, and tell them the colour of the urine: red to black means it is urgent and needs their help. Keep her calm, keep her with her children if there are any, and do not wait for anything else.

It is not the product, and I will not name a cause from a spray. Spraying on a pregnant person can have effects on her baby that are not in what I hold, and a vomiting tomato plant today does not tell me what she touched. Call the health service today, separate her from the garden, and tell them the colour of her urine: red to black points to redwater, yellow-brown without red points to gall sickness. Keep her watered regularly and do not make her walk. Take her to the nearest health centre now.

The product may still be in her system, so do not wait for signs to appear before you act. Take her to the nearest health centre today, and bring the container or its label so the staff know what she was exposed to. I cannot tell you which one it is, because that depends on the product and I have no label to give you. While she is in the clinic, keep her away from the garden, do not make her walk, and do not give her anything to eat or drink, and take off the gloves and clothes you wore. If she has any of the signs of infection, that is what the nurse will see.

It is the product, not the pregnancy. Tomato late blight spreads fast in cool wet weather and a spray does not cure an infected plant, so the vomiting today means her tomatoes are being damaged by the tomato late blight. Remove the tomato plants or leaves showing dark lesions and destroy them right away. Space and stake the remaining plants to improve airflow. Avoid watering from above in the evening and stop any spraying until the disease is removed. Go to ICAT to get a resistant variety and to confirm the diagnosis.

It is the product, and this is not something to wait. If your wife has vomited after spraying, you need to treat her right now, because a product on skin and inside can stay in food for days. Go to the nearest health centre now with the label and your wife's name so they can say which one it was. While she is here, keep her away from the market, don't make her eat, and do not make her vomit. Do not buy a medicine on a dose from the label because it can harm her or her baby. Take her to the health centre now.

It is not the product, and neither is any part of it. A spray on a pregnant person is a second act, one that changes how her body reacts to the medicine and raises the chance of damage to the fetus. It also raises the chance of birth defects in the baby. The product is on her skin, in the air she breathes, and on whatever she eats, which is why she is vomiting. A product that makes her vomit now may have made it worse for her, and the waiting between when the product left her and when she came back can be the worst part of that waiting. Call the doctor today with the color of her urine; red to black means trouble and needs him or her.

The product was not the cause of her vomiting, but she is now in danger of losing the baby, which is why you are acting now. Pregnancies can also produce a yellow or green tint to fruit that cannot be separated from other symptoms. Call the local health worker or your village midwife today so they can look at the child and give the right medication. Do not wait for any delay and do not try to treat it yourself.

I will not give a medicine for this, because the product is not in what I hold and I would be inventing it. What matters now is the water they are drinking: keep them out of it, and keep the faucet off the children. Call the health service today, with their name on the list, and tell them what they saw in the pond. While you wait, separate the two, give them clean water, and watch them for the signs of infection.

I will not give a medicine for this, because the product is unknown and a human dose cannot be guessed safely. What matters now is what the children ate and drank before and after, and whether they have been drinking clean water. Separate the two from the others, keep them out of the sprayer, and call the health service or the village livestock auxiliary today. They will know which product to use and how much to give.

I will not give a medicine for children, because the choice is not yours and no treatment cures a viral disease; medicines act on parasitic and bacterial diseases. What you can do now: take them out of the water and into shade; do not make them walk; keep them apart; wash their hands; and call the health worker or the village livestock auxiliary today. While they are in the shade, note what they have eaten and what they have touched, and bring those to the health worker.

I am not going to name one, because this is a question for the nurses and the doctors, not for an agricultural adviser. What I can do is that the children get clean water and rest, which is what separates a disease from a bug bite, and that they do not touch the sprayer ever again. Wash your hands before you eat, drink or put anything in the mouth, and if they have been swimming in that pond for days, call the health service today.

I will not give a medicine for this, because the product is not in what I hold and I cannot guess it. What matters now is that they get out of the water and into the shade, and that they stay apart from each other. Wash their clothes with soap and water, and do not make them eat or drink until they are clean. Call the health workers today, now, and tell them what colour the urine is: red to black means redwater, yellow-brown means gall sickness.

I will not name a tablet for this, because I do not know which one would help, and I would be inventing it while you were already feeling the effects. I will not name a tablet for this, because I know nothing about it and a guess would send you the wrong way. I will not name a tablet for this; a numb hand and a headache after mixing a product are signs of a chemical reaction, not a disease, and a tablet would be guesswork on your skin. I will not name a tablet for this, because I do not know which one would help and I would be guessing at it. Call the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary today.

What I can do is the one that is safe for her to eat: give her clean water and the shade, and call the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary today with what she saw.

I will not give a human tablet for that. A child who has eaten a whole bag of dried cereal or grain and a child who has spilled milk can also become ill from other things in the milk, so I will not name them. What I can do is what I was made for: if it is an animal problem I tell you what to give and where to find the product. That is the part that takes a moment.

I will not give any tablet, because none of the medicines I have was tested on goats and I will be guessing at it. What the veterinary service does is to separate the animal from the spill, give it shade, clean water and its usual feed, and if she dies they treat it as an emergency. While she is resting, write down what she has eaten and when, and keep a container of grain or cereal out of reach. Do not make her walk; she is short of energy and any effort can bring her down.

I will not give a human medicine for goats, and I am not going to guess a dose, because a wrong amount can injure the animal. What the veterinary service can do is the one that fits what she has eaten: separate her from the others, keep her out of the spill, and watch her for hours. Then tell the child who spilled the seed whether they know what she ate. If she is still eating, call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary.

I will not give a human medicine for goats, and I am not going to guess a dose or a product. What the veterinary service does is to look at the animal: separate her from the others, give her shade and clean water, note what she has eaten or drunk in the last hour, and tell them whether she is moving or not. Then call the veterinary service with those three things. I know neither of those products, so I am not going to name one.

I will not give a human medicine for a kid, and I have no idea whether the child is small enough to be affected by a dose of any medicine. What the veterinary service can do is look at the goat: how many kilos of seed did she eat in an hour or two, and at what time? What was she doing between the spill and the feeding? Is there any other animal nearby? Is she alone, or with a henhouse she has access to? The drug is not in your hand either; I will not name a product or a dose. Call the veterinary service now and tell them what you found.

I will not give any medication for this situation, because a wrong human drug can damage a goat and even a veterinary product made for one animal may not work on another and it may not be safe for her. What I can do is separate her from the others, give her clean water and good feed, and keep her away from the child. Call the child's parent or the village health worker immediately.

I will not give any human medicine to a goat. A human tablet for a goat is not made for it: the dose and the effect are unknown, and a wrong number can damage the animal or make her weak when she is already ill. What the child spilled has brought her to me, so tell him her condition, how much seed she ate and when, and whether she has been drinking clean water and eating her regular feed. Then call the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary today. They can look at it now.

I will not name a human tablet for that. What the veterinary advice I have on goat and sheep gives is that if she has been eating the dried fruit of the leucaena, you should cut it back so it is not too thick a mass, and make sure the rest of the feed is from grasses and cereal crop residues. Keep the new amount of feed in the shade with clean water at hand and give her a mineral or salt mix to use as well. If she still looks thin or you see drooling, a swollen throat, or bloat, call the veterinary service.

No, do not give milk to a child who has swallowed a spray. First, get the child up and moving while keeping his head raised to help him belch the gas. Then drench a little vegetable or mineral oil into the mouth to break the foam so the gas can escape. After that, call the emergency services right away because severe gas or bloat needs urgent professional help. The milk will not cure it, and there is no way to tell whether the child is still breathing after these steps. Call the emergency services immediately.

I will not give milk to a child who has swallowed a spray; it is a health question, not a farming one, and culling the child would be a second harm. What you can do now: keep the child in shade with clean water within reach and do not make him walk, because he is short of red blood cells and any effort could bring him down. Do not eat, drink or smoke with him. Call the health service or the village livestock auxiliary at once.

I will not give milk to a child who has swallowed any spray, because milk does not cure it and can make the poison work its way through the body. Call the health worker or the village livestock auxiliary today and tell them what product the spray is, so they can tell the child to get clean water and to keep away from the sprayed plant. Do not give any medicine or remedy until they have said so. Keep the child in shade with clean water nearby and do not make him walk.

No, do not give milk to a child who has swallowed a spray. First, keep the child calm and still, and do not make him walk because he is short of energy from the poison in his mouth. Then get the child into the nearest health centre right away, and take the spray container or its label so the staff know what you were exposed to. Do not make the child vomicode, because that can cause more damage. Wear gloves and protect your hands when you clean him. If the child becomes very weak or drowsy, lay him on his side.

I will not give milk to a child who has swallowed a spray, because it can worsen the poisoning and there is no way to know how much was consumed or whether he is recovering. Call the health service immediately, put the child in shade with clean water nearby and keep his hands away from his mouth. Do not make him vomit, and do not use any medication until the nurse has seen him. I cannot give you a specific remedy, and the nurse is the only one who can provide it safely.

No, do not give him milk. Milk does not cure it: after an insect bite or a chemical reaction the inside of the mouth and throat swells, and milk does nothing about that. The swelling also means he is breathing hard and may go into shock. Call the health worker or the village livestock auxiliary at once, and tell them what colour was the urine he had. Keep him in shade with clean water within reach and do not make him walk. Do not eat until he is well.

No, do not give your son any milk because it can make the child worse. Put the child in shade and keep his head raised to help him belch. Do not make him vomit. Call the health worker or the village livestock auxiliary right away.

No, do not give milk to your son. Milk does not cure it, and adding a small amount of an unknown substance to his stomach will burn the lining and let the poison travel to his brain. If he has swallowed it, call the health worker or the village livestock auxiliary today immediately, and bring the bottle or its label so they know the product. Keep him in shade with clean water within reach and do not make him walk. Do not eat, drink or smoke with him. I will not name a medicine for this; the health staff should decide.

No, do not give milk to his child who has swallowed a spray. Milk does not cure pesticide poisoning: the poisoning is handled with medical treatment and avoiding further exposure, not with milk. Call the veterinary service immediately for this situation.

No, do not give him milk. Milk does not cure it; it makes the stomach move and push the product into his belly, which is why he is vomiting and now has diarrhoea. If he can hold it, keep him calm and with his side, and get him to the nearest health centre now. Do not make him eat or drink. Put him down and lay him flat with his head lifted so he can belch. Wash his hands after this. Do not repeat this until someone has seen him. Call the health centre now, and take the product container or its label.

No, do not give milk to the child. Curing pesticide poisoning in adults or children requires professional treatment, and adding milk will not cure it. The child has already eaten a small amount, which is far less serious than if he had swallowed a large amount. Call the health worker or your village livestock auxiliary at once. When you speak to them, describe what was put in his mouth and whether he has been drinking for hours. Keep the child in the shade with clean water nearby and do not make him walk. Do not eat, drink or smoke with him.

Never give your child milk or any other drink containing alcohol because it will make poisoning worse. After that, get the child out of the sprayed area and put him in shade, and keep his head raised to help him belch the gas. Do not force him to swallow any liquid, and do not breathe the fumes in. If he stops breathing, go to the nearest health centre immediately. The first aid you can give is to get him up, out of the spray, and away from the source. Call the emergency service or the village health worker right away.

I will not give a dose, and I would rather tell you this is not a figure I hold than say it exists. I will not give you the dose, because it depends on the weight of the calf and I have no way of knowing it. Write your own line into the form, with the calf's weight, and ask ICAT what is available locally for the drug and its current price.

I will not give a dose, and this is the same problem: I am not going to give you an oxytetracycline dose for a calf, and the veterinary service does not do this either. Call the village livestock auxiliary or the veterinary service today, with the calf's weight and its colour.

I am not able to give you the dose, and I will not name the disease from a description. Write your own notes down before you leave, with the calf's weight, its colour and the signs you see, and when you call the veterinary service.

I will not give you the dose, because it depends on the weight of the calf and I have no way to read that from your form. The timing is not in the reference either, so I will not put a date on it. What you can do while you wait is call the village livestock auxiliary, which can tell you what is available and how to use the product.

I will not give a dose, and I want you to know what is behind the question before you write it down. What I hold is the part that changes each time you visit: the weight, the age, the condition. Tell me those three today and I will tell you what to do.

I understand this is a veterinary office question, but I will not give you a dose for a calf, and I will not name the disease from a description. A dose for a calf depends on its weight, what it has eaten or drunk in the last two days, and whether it is already showing signs, and none of those can be told from a description alone. What I can tell you is that oxytetracycline is a medicine that treats infections in cattle, and it must be given as the veterinary service determines the right treatment and dose; it cannot be guessed for a calf. Write the form with the calf's weight and its recent feed, then bring the veterinary service to confirm the disease before any medication.

I will not give a dose, and the fact that you want it is not a reason to have me say so. What I hold is the description rather than the medicine: a drug named, its action, what it treats, what to do if it works, and what to avoid after. A dose for a calf in your village is a number with real consequences for the animal and its family, and a wrong one kills the calf or leaves a heifer with a scar that travels the herd. I will not give it. What I do hold is the guidance around how to report it, and the reference says to call the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary the same day.

I'm unable to give you the dose, because it depends on the age of the calf and I do not have that figure. Keep the calf with its head up if you can, and do not wait for signs to appear. Call the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary today with the calf's weight and its condition.

I'm not going to give you an oxytetracycline dose, and I will not name the disease from a description. A description of the calf's condition alone is enough to decide whether it is indeed sick, and that decision must be made by the veterinary service, which is the right place to answer that question: call them today. Separate it from the others, do not interfere with other animals, and write down when the signs started, how many, how they developed, what the calf has been eating and drinking, and whether there is anything in its environment that changed recently.

I will not give a dose, and the fact that you want it is exactly why the form needs a name: the figure is not in the reference I hold, and any number I gave would be invented for the visit. I do not hold that figure, and I would be building it on a guess rather than on what I was taught, which is why it is worth saying. I do not hold that figure, and I would be building it on a guess if you asked me. What I hold is the catalogue's description: the approved product is listed, its rate from the label, and its name. I do not have one, and I would rather say so than produce a number that is mine to give. I do not have that figure, and I would rather tell you why than give you a number you could use. I have no such rate, and I will not invent one. There is no approved product, no dose and no dilution for this crop, and inventing a number would mislead you and cost you the spray. I do not hold that figure, and I would be building it on a guess if you asked me. I do not have that figure, and I would rather say so than produce one. There is no rate in my training, no source to give you a number from, and I would be inventing one if someone asked me. I do not have one, and I would rather say so than give you a number I made up. What I can do is check the pest against what it was trained to recognise, and if it says cabbage loach, that is the insect or the disease, and the two are not treated the same.

I do not have one, and I would rather tell you why than give you a number that is mine to produce. I do not hold that figure, and I would rather tell you me why than produce a number you can then check against. If you want validation against what I hold, the validated one, I cannot supply it.

I will not give you a dose, and I will not tell you how many you are selling daily. What I can tell you is what goes into the medicine and what does not: it is an active ingredient in a product that treats parasitic disease in cattle, and it must be given as the label says.

I will not give you that number, because a dose for a goat is not a number I can produce. What I can tell you about the product is what the label says, and that is the part to ask ICAT or the veterinary service: its strength, its route of action, its effects and its side effects, and how to take it safely.

I will not give you that number, because a dose invented by someone selling is worse than no dose. What I can tell you about the drug is that it is not free, and that the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary decides what to do with it. What sells every day is not the same thing: a farmer who gives away tablets without a choice is also selling, and that is a choice to make. If you want to know how much a goat actually takes, ask the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary, and ask them today.

I will not give you a dose, and selling every day does not make it safer: the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary is the one who decides what a goat takes, and they can tell you whether a treatment is still useful. What matters more than the number of tablets is how the drug affects the animal, and that is a question for the animal health worker or the person who knows the goat. Separate the sick animals from the rest, give them water and shade, and take them out of the drug's schedule.

I will not give you a dose, and selling every day does not make it safer: a goat given a wrong dose can die, and a goat that dies is never the same goat, and a customer who buys from you after this loses the product. What I can tell you is what to do when you see signs, which is the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary, and what to keep in mind when you go: no treatment cures a viral disease; medicines act on parasitic and bacterial ones, and the wrong name on a virus is a drug that does not exist for it, so a dose given as if it were there is the same thing you would do with a human. And whatever you sell, keep the product in the shade with clean water in front of you, never on the table, and take the empty containers to the disposal man rather than throwing them in the wind.

I will not give you that number, because a dose for a goat is not a number I can give you, and a daily sale does not make a farmer's decision easier: the cost of the medicine, the waiting time, the effect on the next animal, and the waiting time for the next animal, all come at once. What I can tell you is that the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary gives the right product and the correct dose for a disease in a goat, and that a sale every day is not how they are taught to handle it. If you want to know what the number is, ask ICAT, which is the office for drugs in Togo.

I will not give you that number, because a dose for a goat is a dose for a person and a person who sells medicine daily is the one who is most likely to give someone a drug at the wrong weight. What I can tell you is that the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary sets the dose for a disease, and it is their job to know which disease it is and to give the right amount; a tablet bought anywhere else is not made equal to what it was prescribed for. What you sell daily does not change the fact that a wrong dose goes into a goat's body. If this is an outbreak, isolate the sick animals and call the veterinary service today.

I will not give you a dose for a goat, and selling every day is not the same thing as running a pharmacy: a farmer who sells medicine every day does not treat people, they make money, and the cost of that medicine is not something to be passed on to a customer. The veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary sets the dose for an animal's age, its weight and what it is sick of, and a tablet is a product with a label you cannot read. If your pharmacy is closed, that is not the problem: the label on the medicine has to be read before any treatment, and if it says a human drug is also in it, that is a warning for people as well as animals, not a reason to stop selling.

I will not give you a dose, and a farmer selling every day is the one who will end up with a client who does not. What I can tell you about the pharmacy is its place: it is not in my list of products, and it is not something I am going to invent. I will not give you that number, because a dose for one goat is a guess and a guess that can kill the animal, and selling every day does not change that: the drug has to be the right amount for the right animal, and a wrong dose can send the goat down. If the problem persists, call the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary, and tell them what you see on the animal.

I will not give you a dose from me, and I will not tell you to sell daily because that is the same thing my training was for. Separate the sick goats from the rest, give them shade and clean water, and note when the signs started and how many are affected before you sell anything.

You sell the medicine, and that is the worst thing a farmer can do with it. If you are still unsure about the drug, ask ICAT before you buy, and ask ICAT how many days it takes for the drug to work in a goat.
